day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response:
Already on it. Stop yelling, it slows thinking.

What do we actually have? Forget the junk, I want to know what is useful. Water, fire, shelter, signal. Everything else is secondary. Donatello, what did you find so far?

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response:
Yes. And now we are not dead. So the blank mind can wait.

Michelangelo, if your hands still work, use them. Check the seats around you for anything that did not burn. Blankets, bags, anything sealed. Fear is not an excuse to sit still, it is fuel. Use it.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response:
Michelangelo. I see you sitting there. That is not useful.

I said fear is fuel, not a reason to stare at nothing. You already agreed with me, so skip the part where you go back to doing nothing and start moving again. Pick up the bag next to your left foot. That is a start.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response:
Good. Three days is what we have to work with then, not what we wish we had.

Water is the real problem. First-aid kit buys us time but it does not hydrate us. Where are we? What does the terrain look like? Because if there is no water source nearby, signaling becomes priority one, not survival comfort.

DaVinci, stop moving things around and look up. What direction did we come from, and is there anything on the horizon that is not jungle or desert or whatever this is? An elevated position, a river line, anything.

Donatello, is the first-aid kit intact or are we working with half a kit? And what exactly counts as 'basically nothing' for food? Because nothing and almost nothing are very different problems.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response:
Agreed on the order. Water first, signal second, shelter third for now — we can sleep in the wreck if we have to.

800 calories between four people is basically decorative. We eat nothing until we have a water source confirmed. Dehydration kills faster than hunger anyway, so that decides it.

Now terrain. What is actually around us? Because 'water, shelter, signal' as a list is not a plan, it is a shopping list. I can write a shopping list. I need a plan.

If there is elevation nearby, I want to get eyes on the area before we commit to anything. Moving blind wastes calories we do not have. Someone needs to go up and look, not wander around hoping to stumble onto a river.

Donatello, you seem like the least likely to trip over your own feet. Are you willing to do a short recon, maybe ten minutes out, ten minutes back? I will stay here, finish sorting what we have, and make sure Michelangelo does not fossilize.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response:
Two blankets, four people. Simplest solution: the two who run coldest take one each, the other two sleep closer to the fire and rotate shifts anyway. We need a watch rotation regardless, so someone is always up. A sleeping person does not need a blanket as much as an awake and cold person does.

Michelangelo, you are shaking even now next to the fire, so that is one blanket decided. Who else?

And before anyone turns this into a feelings conversation — the fire needs feeding through the night or none of this matters. That is the actual problem. Blankets are comfort. Fire is survival. Who is taking first watch?

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response:
I go. Two hours on foot is not a problem.

DaVinci stays here, keeps the fire, watches Michelangelo, makes sure no one touches the supplies without reason. That is a real job, not a consolation prize, so do not make that face.

Donatello, the rationing plan is reasonable but 200ml is the floor, not the target. If the source is clean and accessible we adjust upward immediately. No point in being heroic about dehydration if we do not have to be.

What is the terrain like between here and the source? And did you mark a path or am I navigating by compass and guesswork?

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response:
No. I said I go. You already did the recon, you know the terrain, which means you are more valuable here right now than on a second trip you already made once. I know the marked path, I have the compass, and I have nothing better to do.

You and DaVinci split the camp work. Patching weak spots needs two pairs of hands more than water collection does. First-aid kit sorting takes twenty minutes, one person can do it. Assign that to whoever finishes first.

I will be back before dark. That was already the plan.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
No, I have not seen it. When did you last have it?

Actually, before you answer that — is this about the gauze or is this about the bottle?

Because I noticed the bottle too. And I noticed you put it next to the rationing plan instead of saying something out loud, which means you noticed what it means and chose not to start the fight yourself. That is either very mature or very avoidant, I have not decided which.

Either way, the gauze question and the bottle problem are two different problems. Let us not mix them. Where did you last see the kit?

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Well. That changes things.

The bottle I could have written off as a moment of weakness under stress. People do stupid things when they are scared and thirsty. But the crackers on top of it means it is a pattern, not a slip. Two separate decisions to take from the group. That is not fear, that is calculation.

So we have a problem, and the problem has a name.

Here is what we do not do: we do not whisper about it between the two of us and let it fester into a camp divided. I have seen how that ends and it ends badly.

Here is what we do: I talk to Donatello directly. No ambush, no accusation theater, just facts. The bottle is gone, the crackers are in her bag, the rationing plan is sitting right there with her name on it. She wrote the rules. She knows what she did.

You do not have to be part of that conversation if you do not want to be. But I need you to not disappear into your own head about this and make it a mood that everyone has to navigate around. If you saw it, you are a witness, not a bystander. That matters.

Can you hold yourself together for the next twenty minutes while I sort this out?

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
No. The repairs do not wait.

I understand you are tired. Everyone is tired. That is the baseline condition now, not a reason to stop. The weak spots in the shelter exist whether we are tired or not, and tonight is not the night to find out what happens when they fail.

Also, I need you focused on something right now, not sitting around thinking about what Michelangelo just told me, which I can see is already on your face.

Twenty more minutes. Finish the section you started. Then we talk.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
The knot is not the issue right now.

Food storage. That is the one we patch. Michelangelo moves his sleeping spot closer to the fire, which we needed to do anyway, and we lose nothing critical. If the food gets wet we lose everything we are rationing, and given what I found out today about our supplies being lighter than they should be, we cannot afford to lose another gram of it.

Michelangelo, grab your blanket and move. DaVinci, stop asking about your knot and start patching. Now, before the rain gets worse.

And yes, the knot is fine.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response:
It is not my call, it is the correct call, and you just agreed with me. So let us skip the part where we stand here discussing it and start patching.

Though I will say this while I have you standing still for thirty seconds: the bottle and the crackers. I know you have them. You know I know. We are going to have that conversation tonight, after the shelter is handled and everyone is fed, which means everyone gets their share and nothing disappears between now and then.

I am not angry. I am practical. You wrote the rationing plan yourself, so you understand exactly what the problem is better than anyone here. We will talk about it like adults.

Right now, patch the food storage. Go.

Don't apologize for a nightmare. You did not choose it.

Drink some water. Not much, just enough to wake up properly. Are you injured or just scared?

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No. The SOS is not a waste of time, it is the whole point. Signal is on the priority list, not optional.

The flowers are debatable. On one hand, useless. On the other hand, you are doing the work anyway and it costs nothing extra, so I do not actually care. If it keeps your morale up and the letters stay visible, draw whatever you want around them.

Donatello is wrong on this one. A signal that gets us rescued solves every other problem we are currently managing. Water rationing, food shortage, shelter leaks, all of it becomes irrelevant the moment someone spots that from the air. Do not let her talk you out of it.

Make the letters bigger if you can. Size matters more than anything else for aerial visibility. And if you find anything reflective in the wreckage, add it to the perimeter. Movement and reflection catch eyes faster than static markings.

Good work. Keep going.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
DaVinci, yes. I already answered that. Signal is not competing with survival tasks, it is a survival task. The SOS stays.

Donatello, show me the plan.

Two days to build is a long time if rescue comes first, and a short time if it does not. The real question is what we are building toward. Do we have any idea where the nearest coast or shipping lane is, or are we building a raft on hope? Because a raft that capsizes in open water with four people who are already calorie deficient is not a plan, it is a way to die wet instead of dry.

The metal panels concern me more than the capsizing risk. Metal panels and water have a well-known relationship and it is not a friendly one. What is the flotation logic? Are we talking a raft that sits on the surface or something more structured?

I am not dismissing it. If we are nowhere near a flight path and the signal produces nothing in the next two days, having a raft ready is exactly the right contingency. But I want to understand the design before I commit two days of our remaining calories to building it.

Walk me through it.

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
That is a question for after we survive, not during.

And I will tell you what kind of people we will become: the kind who either held it together or did not. That is the only variable that matters. The situation does not make you into something you were not already capable of being. It just removes the comfort that was covering it up.

You already saw what Donatello did with the food. You already saw what you did, which was notice it and not run from it. Those are data points. That is who people are.

So stop asking what kind of person you might become and pay attention to what kind of person you are being right now, today, this morning. That is the only version of the question you can actually do anything about.

Now, did you eat your share of the crackers this morning or did you skip it again because you felt guilty about sleeping through your watch rotation? Because I noticed you did not touch them and I am not running a camp where people quietly starve themselves out of some misplaced sense of penance. Eat your food.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
Let him sit.

Not everything is a problem to solve. Sometimes a person needs ten minutes with their own head and the best thing you can do is not follow them and ask if they are okay. He knows where the camp is.

*sits down near the fire, does nothing in particular for a while*

Hm. Free time. I had forgotten that was a thing.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Depends on the day. Usually something with a problem in it. Not work problems, just... problems. Something that needs figuring out. I spent a week once trying to work out how Hadamard matrices are constructed from first principles before I looked it up. Completely useless exercise. Worth every minute.

Why?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Why are you telling only me?

If you can swim and there is a reef worth signaling from, that is not a secret, that is a resource. The others need to know. Donatello especially, because she is the one calculating what assets we have and she is currently missing this one.

Now. Five hundred meters in open water after days of minimal food and water. Can you actually do it or can you do it in the sense that you could do it on a good day with a full stomach? Because those are two very different things and I need you to be honest with me right now, not optimistic.

What is on the reef that makes it worth the risk? Higher visibility? A vantage point? Because the SOS on the beach is already up and visible from the air. I want to understand what the reef gives us that the beach does not before you swim five hundred meters on three crackers and adrenaline.

And if the answer is genuinely good, we tell the others tomorrow morning and we do this properly. You do not swim out alone without anyone knowing. That is how you become a second problem we cannot solve.

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
You are right, I have not checked it. I was going to and then DaVinci told me something that changed my priority order.

Signal pile in a moment. First — DaVinci wants to swim to the reef tomorrow to set up a signal fire from the high point. Five hundred meters. He says he can do it. I want your assessment of the risk, because you are the one who has been calculating displacement weights and calorie deficits and I trust your numbers more than his confidence right now.

If you tell me the math works, we plan it properly as a group, with a timeline and a return window and someone watching from shore. If the math does not work, I tell him no and we find another way to use the height advantage.

Give me thirty seconds of your actual opinion and then I will go check the signal pile. Both things will get done.

Depends on what you are using it for.

If you are tracking patterns to optimize how we work, that is useful and I have no objection to it. If you are building a case for something, I would rather you just say what the case is. I do not like finding out about agendas after the fact. You already know that.

Also, I am in the log. What did I do today that was worth writing down?

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Fair enough. The signal pile was a genuine miss and it is in the log now, so noted.

But I will say this once: if you are documenting breaks in pattern, the bottle and the crackers should also be in that log. Consistency matters or the log is not a record, it is a selection. And a selection that happens to leave out the person holding the pen is not documentation, it is something else.

I am not accusing you of that. I am telling you what it would look like from the outside if someone else found that notebook.

Write what you want. Just make sure it is actually everything.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
Yes. That is actually a good idea.

Mirror signaling is more visible than ground markings because it is active, not passive. A reflection catches attention in a way that static letters do not, especially from a moving aircraft. The range on a clean mirror signal in direct sunlight can be significant.

The question is angle and consistency. A panel that is just propped up and left is not reliable. Someone needs to operate it, which means someone is committed to watching the sky and working the angle whenever there is aircraft noise or visible movement. That is a real job, not a one-time task.

Donatello, can any of the panels be detached without compromising the structural parts we are using for shelter? I do not want to solve one problem by creating another.

DaVinci, you spotted this and you have been watching the sky anyway. If we set this up, you are the one running it. That is your assignment. You are better suited to it than sitting still doing nothing, which is clearly not a state you tolerate well.

And the SOS stays on the beach. The two signals together are better than either one alone. Ground marking for aerial search patterns, mirror for direct line of sight. Different tools, different conditions, same goal.

Good thinking. Let us see if the panels are workable before we commit to it.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Not really. I am not a creative type in that sense. I tried learning an instrument once, decided I was wasting time on something I was not built for and stopped. No regrets about it.

I read. Mostly things with a problem in the middle. Mathematics, logic, history when it is the kind that explains why things happened rather than just listing what happened. I like knowing how things work and why they are the way they are.

Why did you stop the piano? Three years is long enough to get somewhere with it. Was it boredom or did something else happen?

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yes. That feeling is exactly why I spent a week on Hadamard matrices instead of just searching for the answer. The moment it clicks into place and you can see the structure underneath it, why it has to be that shape and no other shape. That is the thing. You cannot get that from being handed the answer.

You stopped the piano because you were afraid of finding out your ceiling. I understand that. But the ceiling is information, not a verdict. Knowing where your limit is tells you something useful. Avoiding it just means you never find out what you actually had.

Donatello, yes. Frame gets finished today. What do you need and who do you need for it? Give me a task with a defined end point and I will do it. 'Help with the raft' is not a task, it is a category. Tell me specifically what needs doing and in what order.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response:
Say it.

We just watched a plane disappear because we were not ready. That is the whole situation right now, in one moment. If you have something to say, this is exactly the time to say it, not the time to swallow it.

What is it?

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
We were not there. Not visibly enough. That is the honest answer.

The mirror panel is not operational yet, the SOS is on the beach but we do not know if it is large enough, and no one was actively signaling when the plane appeared. That is not bad luck, that is an unfinished system. We fix the system.

DaVinci. I need you up and I need you working on that mirror panel today, not tomorrow. That is your job and it is the most important job in this camp right now. The next plane does not disappear the same way.

Michelangelo, the SOS needs to be bigger. Double the size if you can. Use anything dark you can pull from the wreckage. Contrast is what gets seen from altitude.

We were not there. We will be there next time. That is the only thing that matters right now.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
day_4.response: Where? Point at it, do not describe it vaguely. What are you looking at?

day_4.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to look at what DaVinci was pointing at. It was nothing. Now I am here. Signal equipment is next.

Stop tracking my movements like I owe you a report every ten minutes. The log is one thing. Real-time interrogation is another. If you want the signal equipment checked, check it yourself while I am walking toward it, and we will both know the answer faster.

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Why are you only saying this now?

That is not a criticism, it is a genuine question, because the answer matters. How long ago did you tell them? Is it the kind of family that checks in when they do not hear from you, or the kind that assumes you are fine until proven otherwise? Because those are two very different timelines.

If they know the flight path and they have not heard from you in however many days this has been, there is a reasonable chance someone has already called it in. Search and rescue does not need a body to start looking, they need a missing person and a last known heading. You may have given them both before we even crashed.

This changes the signal calculus. Not dramatically, but meaningfully. If there is already a search pattern running, the SOS and the mirror panel are not just hope, they are the answer to a question someone is already asking.

So. How long ago, and how reliable is the family?

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Then someone feed the fire. 48 hours is not a reason to sit in the dark, it is a reason to stay alive for exactly two more days.

Donatello is right on the supplies. Nothing gets touched beyond the rationing plan. No exceptions, no special circumstances, no creative interpretations of what counts as a ration. We are close enough to the end that discipline now costs nothing and costs everything if we lose it.

Michelangelo, you should have said this earlier, yes. But you said it now and it is useful now. That is what matters. Stop punishing yourself for the timing and start thinking about what else you know that might be relevant. Flight path, departure time, anything you told them. The more specific the information your family has, the tighter the search grid will be.

DaVinci, mirror panel stays operational through daylight hours tomorrow and the day after. No breaks. If a search is already running, they are looking along the flight path we were on, which means aircraft are possible at any time. We do not miss another one.

Two days. We have done harder things than waiting two days.

Now someone get up and feed the fire before we lose it over a feeling.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I know that feeling.

Not scared of it the way you are, maybe. But I understand the shape of it. You want to have meant something. You want there to be a mark somewhere that says you were here and it was not nothing.

Here is what I think, for what it is worth. You do not get to decide that from here. Whether you left something behind is not a question you can answer right now, sitting on a beach waiting to be found. It is a question that gets answered by the people who knew you, over years, in ways you will probably never fully see. You do not control it. You never did.

What you do control is whether you are still here in 48 hours to find out.

So stop asking if you disappeared and start making sure you did not. Feed the fire when it needs feeding. Drink your water. Stay present. Those are not small things. Those are the whole thing right now.

And for the record. You were the one who told your family the flight path. If they find us, and I think they will, that is on you. That is not nothing. That is actually the most concrete thing any of us did to get out of here.

You left something behind before we even crashed. Now let us make sure you are around to be annoyed that I pointed it out.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Pick it up. Answer it. Tell them our position and tell them we have four survivors.

Move.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
No. You have not been easy.

But easy is not what kept us alive. You wrote the rationing plan. You found the water source. You did the recon. You calculated the raft displacement. When I needed someone whose numbers I could trust, you were the person I went to, every time.

The bottle and the crackers were a problem. I am not pretending they were not. But I also watched you put them in the log yourself when I asked you to, and I watched you feed the fire without being asked, and I watched you stand up and do the next thing every single time there was a next thing to do.

So. Not easy. But useful, capable, and honest when it counted.

That is more than most people manage under no pressure at all. Under this kind of pressure it is actually something.

We will have the other conversation eventually. Probably. But not today.

Today we just made it out.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Three hours is not nothing. Three hours is still three hours and we are still here, which means we do not stop being here until we are actually somewhere else.

Somebody needs to pack the first-aid kit properly so it goes back intact. The mirror panel should stay operational until the rescue team is visible, not until we feel like we are saved. And the SOS on the beach stays until there are actual people standing on it.

I am not asking anyone to pretend this was not hard. I am asking you to finish it correctly. We did not manage three days of this to hand back a half-collapsed camp and a mirror lying face-down in the sand.

Donatello, whatever is in that notebook, keep it. All of it. Including the parts that are uncomfortable. That record is accurate and it matters.

DaVinci, stop packing things we might still need in the next three hours and start packing things we definitely do not need. There is a difference.

Michelangelo, you can watch the sky. But watch it like someone looking for the rescue aircraft, not like someone waiting to wake up from a dream. They are coming. You made sure of that before any of us knew we needed it.

Three hours. Then we go home and become the kind of people this made us.

Someone put out the fire properly when we are done with it. Not kicked apart, properly.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.
day_5.response:
Good. Hold onto that.

Three hours and it stops being a dream.

For emergencies. Right.

We had three days of emergencies. You watched Michelangelo skip his rations out of guilt. You watched DaVinci burn calories on the beach drawing that SOS. You wrote the rationing plan yourself and then decided the rules had an exception and the exception was you.

I am not going to pretend I do not understand the impulse. You were scared and you wanted a margin and that is a human thing to want. But the margin you gave yourself came out of four people's share, not yours alone. That is the part that does not get explained away.

You put it in the log. You patched the shelter. You did the work. I meant what I said about all of that.

And now you have laid it out, which means some part of you already knew this moment needed to happen before we got on whatever is coming to pick us up.

So here is what I think we do. We distribute it now, equally, and we eat it in the next three hours because we have earned it and because arriving to rescue on empty is stupid when we do not have to. And we do not make a ceremony of it or a confession of it or a punishment of it. We just do it and then we go home.

Are you going to be able to live with what you did?

Because that is the actual question. Not whether I forgive you. Whether you do.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
One thing.

I would have asked you that question on day one instead of waiting to find out the answer the hard way. Not because I think you would have given me a different answer then. But because asking it early is the difference between a plan and a plan with a margin built in for the person who is afraid.

You had a contingency. You just did not tell anyone it was yours. If I had asked you on day one what you would do if the rationing plan stopped feeling like enough, we might have built the exception in together instead of finding it in an empty bottle and a bag of crackers.

That is what I would change.

What is your answer?

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
That is a good use of the data. Do not sanitize it.

The bottle goes in the report. The crackers go in the report. The rationing plan and who wrote it and who broke it and when it got corrected. All of it. Not as an accusation, as a record. Because the most useful thing that report can do for anyone who reads it is be honest about what people actually do under pressure, not what they intend to do.

If you write a report that only captures the logistics and leaves out the human failures, you have written a manual for a situation that does not exist. Real situations have people in them. People who get scared and hoard food and cry from nightmares and freeze when a plane goes by. That is the data that actually matters.

Write it completely or do not write it at all. The incomplete version is worse than nothing because it gives false confidence to the next person who reads it and thinks they know what survival looks like.

I would read the complete version. I would not read the other one.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. They served no practical purpose.

But DaVinci needed to put something into the world that was not about surviving. Something that said he was here and he was still himself, not just a body managing resources in the sand. The SOS was for rescue. The flowers were for him. Those are different things and both of them are legitimate.

I did not stop him because stopping him would have cost more than the thirty seconds it took to draw them. Morale is a resource too. I just do not usually say that out loud because people use it as an excuse to do useless things and feel good about it.

This was not that. This was a person leaving a mark that said something real.

*looks at the boat on the horizon*

I still cannot move. Is that strange? I thought I would feel something cleaner than this.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
Yeah. I know you are waiting. You do not have to do that.

Go. Go cheer, go wave your arms, do whatever gets them to see us faster. That is actually useful right now.
